title: My ideal holiday, with the conditional

tips.title: Si plus imperfect, then conditional
tips.body: *Si j'avais assez d'argent, j'irais au Japon.* In an *if* sentence about a dream, **si** takes the **imperfect**, never the conditional and never the future: *si j'aurais* is wrong there. (When *si* means *whether*, as in *je ne savais pas si j'aurais le temps*, the rule does not apply.)

tips.title: Conditional is future stem plus imperfect endings
tips.body: Take the future stem, which ends in **-r**, and add *ais, ais, ait, ions, iez, aient*. So *j'irai* is *I will go* and *j'irais* is *I would go*: one letter apart, and the examiners look for it.

tips.title: J'aimerais and je voudrais are conditionals
tips.body: They already mean *I would like*, so they carry the politeness on their own. Follow either with an **infinitive**: *j'aimerais visiter*, *je voudrais rester*.

tips.title: Build the conditional from the future
tips.body: You already know the conditional if you know the future: take the **same stem** and add the **imperfect endings**. *J’irai* becomes *j’irais*, *je serai* becomes *je serais*. No new stems to learn, and the dream is one letter from the plan.

tips.title: Si j'avais un marteau: the dream pattern
tips.body: Remember the old French song *Si j'avais un marteau* (If I had a hammer): *si* + the imperfect *avais*, then a conditional in the other half. Every dream sentence copies that shape: *si j'avais le choix, j'irais au Japon*.

why.matters: The ideal holiday is a favourite exam task because it forces a tense you have not needed yet: the conditional, for what you *would* do. It is the future stem with the imperfect endings, so anyone who has both tenses already has this one, and the irregular stems are the same as the future's. The topic exists for the dream, *j'aimerais, je voudrais, ce serait*, for the sentence that carries it, *si* with the imperfect and then the conditional, and for the contrast that shows control: reality in the present, the dream in the conditional, *mais* between them.

examples.title: J'irais: the future stem with the imperfect endings
examples.body: *Aller* has the irregular future stem *ir-*, and the conditional simply borrows it and adds the imperfect endings: *j'irais, tu irais, il irait, nous irions, vous iriez, ils iraient*. The picture shows both parts at once, and the same trick works for every verb: *je serais, j'aurais, je ferais, je pourrais, je voudrais*. Build the conditional from the future, and there is nothing new to learn except the meaning.

visual.alt: A conjugation table of aller in the conditional with the future stem ir drawn apart from the imperfect endings ais, ais, ait, ions, iez and aient

examples.title: J'irai or j'irais: one letter
examples.body: *J'irai* is *I will go* and *j'irais* is *I would go*, and the whole difference is the *s*. In the dictation it is silent, so the grammar decides it: a plan takes the future, a dream takes the conditional. *J'aimerais, je voudrais* and *je préférerais* are all conditionals, which is why they sound polite: they are wishes, not demands, and they open every ideal-holiday paragraph.

I would go to the Maldives
I would like to go alone

Si j'étais riche, je louerais une villa.* Never a conditional after *si* meaning *if*. Set the dream against the real thing, *d'habitude nous allons en Espagne, mais si j'avais le choix …*, and one sentence shows the present, the imperfect and the conditional.

steps.title: Les vacances de rêve
steps.body:
The ideal holiday is a favourite exam task because it forces a tense you have not used yet: the **conditional**, for what you *would* do. First the words for dreaming big.

*Idéal* agrees: *mes vacances idéales*, feminine plural, because *vacances* is feminine and always plural. *De rêve* (of dreams) never changes: *des vacances de rêve*, *un hôtel de rêve*.

visuals.fallback: Les vacances de rêve: mes vacances idéales — my ideal holiday; des vacances de rêve — a dream holiday; une île — an island; une île déserte — a desert island; un hôtel de luxe — a luxury hotel; cinq étoiles — five-star; une croisière — a cruise; faire le tour du monde — to travel around the world; un safari — a safari; découvrir — to discover; explorer — to explore; se détendre — to relax; se reposer — to rest; ne rien faire — to do nothing; loin de tout — far from everything; sans mes parents — without my parents

check.solution: *Des vacances de rêve*: plural, and *de rêve* never changes.
accepted: des vacances de rêve
des vacances de reve

steps.title: The conditional: would
steps.body:
The **conditional** says what *would* happen. It is built from two things you already know:

**the future stem** + **the imperfect endings** (*-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*).

*rester* → *je resterais* (I would stay) · *visiter* → *nous visiterions* (we would visit) · *partir* → *je partirais*.

The irregular stems are exactly the future ones: *aller* → *j'irais*, *être* → *je serais* / *ce serait*, *avoir* → *j'aurais* / *il y aurait*, *faire* → *je ferais*, *pouvoir* → *je pourrais*, *vouloir* → *je voudrais*.

Future and conditional look alike, so read the ending: *j'irai* (future, I will go) against *j'irais* (conditional, I would go). One letter, a different tense.

On the Pearson specification only *je voudrais* (I would like) is needed at both tiers; the other conditionals, including *j'aimerais* and *si* + imperfect sentences, are Higher tier only.

visuals.alt: The conditional of aller: j'irais, tu irais, il irait, nous irions, vous iriez, ils iraient
A table contrasting the future and the conditional of the same verbs

check.prompt: Write the French for **I would go** (from *aller*).
check.solution: Stem *ir-* plus *-ais*: **j'irais**. *J'irai*, without the *s*, is the future.
accepted: j'irais

steps.title: J'aimerais, je voudrais, ce serait
steps.body:
Three conditionals carry most of the topic, and they take an **infinitive** straight after them:

- **j'aimerais** + infinitive: *j'aimerais visiter le Japon* — I would like to visit Japan
- **je voudrais** + infinitive: *je voudrais faire une croisière* — I would like to go on a cruise
- **je préférerais** + infinitive: *je préférerais me reposer* — I would prefer to rest

And for describing the dream: **ce serait** (it would be) and **il y aurait** (there would be). *Ce serait parfait; il y aurait une plage privée.*

*Je voudrais* is also the polite request in every role play — *je voudrais réserver une chambre* — which is why the next topics keep coming back to it.

steps.text: *Je voudrais rester dans un hôtel de luxe.*
*Il y aurait une piscine et un spa.*

check.solution: *Je voudrais* takes the **infinitive** straight after it: *je voudrais faire*.
options: Je voudrais que faire une croisière

steps.title: Si + imperfect, conditional
steps.body:
A dream is usually *if*: *if I were rich, I would…*. French has a fixed pattern for it:

**si + imperfect, then conditional.**

*Si j'étais riche, j'irais aux Maldives.* · *Si je pouvais, je ferais le tour du monde.* · *Si j'avais le choix, je partirais sans mes parents.*

Compare the real-plan version from earlier: **si + present, then future** (*si j'ai assez d'argent, j'irai*). The tense after *si* decides how likely the thing is: present for a real possibility, imperfect for a dream.

What never happens in an *if* sentence: a future or a conditional straight after *si*. *Si j'aurais* and *si j'aurai* are both wrong there. (When *si* means *whether*, as in *je ne savais pas si j'aurais le temps*, it can take either.)

steps.body: The task will give bullets: where, with whom, accommodation, activities, why. Every verb in the conditional, one *si* clause somewhere, and a reason at the end.

*Nous resterions dans un hôtel de luxe et il y aurait une piscine.*
*Je ferais de la plongée tous les jours et je ne ferais rien d'autre.*
*Si je pouvais, je resterais un mois entier.*

steps.title: Why it would be perfect: reasons and preferences
steps.body:
The top-band marks come from **justifying**, and the conditional gives you elegant ways to do it.

- **parce que / car** + conditional: *ce serait parfait parce que je pourrais me reposer*.
- **plutôt que de** + infinitive (rather than): *je préférerais explorer plutôt que de bronzer*.
- **au lieu de** + infinitive (instead of): *au lieu de rester à l'hôtel, je découvrirais la ville*.
- **ne… jamais / ne… rien** in the conditional: *je ne resterais jamais dans un camping*; *je ne ferais rien*.

Notice the comparison hiding in a preference: *je préférerais X plutôt que Y* is the conditional version of *je préfère X parce que…* from the last topic.

steps.title: Going deeper: dream against reality, and the two meanings of would
steps.body:
**Contrast the dream with the real thing.** *D'habitude, nous allons en Espagne avec mes parents et c'est bien, mais si j'avais le choix, je partirais sans eux.* Present for reality, conditional for the dream, *mais* between them: that one sentence shows tense control the examiner can mark.

**English *would* has two meanings.** *I would go to the Maldives* (dream) is the conditional, *j'irais*. But *when I was little, we would go to the beach* (past habit) is the **imperfect**, *nous allions*. Translating that second *would* with a conditional is a classic translation error.

**Keep the if-rule firm.** When *si* means *if*: present or imperfect after it, never future, never conditional. (When *si* means *whether*, as in *je ne savais pas si j'aurais le temps*, the rule does not apply.)

**Range that costs nothing.** *Il y aurait*, *je pourrais*, *ne… rien*, *plutôt que de*, *au lieu de*.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Conditional** = future stem + imperfect endings: *je resterais, nous visiterions, ils iraient*. Irregular stems as in the future: *ir-, ser-, aur-, fer-, pourr-, voudr-, verr-*.
- **Future or conditional**: *j'irai* (will) against *j'irais* (would). Read the ending.
- **J'aimerais / je voudrais / je préférerais** + infinitive. **Ce serait**, **il y aurait**.
- **Si + imperfect, conditional** for a dream; **si + present, future** for a real plan. Never future or conditional after *si* meaning *if*.
- **Justify**: *parce que*, *plutôt que de*, *au lieu de*, *ne… jamais*, *ne… rien*.
- **Dream against reality**: present for what you do, conditional for what you would do, *mais* between them.
- **Past-habit *would*** is the imperfect, not the conditional.

examTechnique.body:
The ideal holiday is set because it demands the conditional, and the conditional is one of the tenses the top band is marked on. Every verb in the description should be conditional, with at least one irregular stem, and there should be one *si + imperfect* sentence. The examiner is also listening for *j'aimerais* and *je voudrais* with an infinitive, and for *il y aurait*.

Two traps decide the grade. After *si* meaning *if*, never the conditional or the future. And English *would* is the conditional only when it means a wish; when it means *used to*, French wants the imperfect. In writing, contrast the dream with real holidays so the present and the conditional appear side by side, and end with a reason.
examinerErrors: *Si j'aurais* or *si j'aurai*: after *si*, the imperfect (dream) or the present (plan).
Writing the future for the conditional: *j'irai* when *j'irais* is meant, so the dream reads as a plan.
Translating a past-habit *would* with the conditional: *nous irions* for *we would go every summer*.
*Je voudrais que faire* or *je voudrais fais*: *je voudrais* takes the infinitive directly.
*Mes vacances idéales serait*: *vacances* is plural, so *seraient*.
Describing without justifying, so the answer never reaches the band that asks why.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer runs the whole description in an accurate conditional with irregular stems, includes a si + imperfect sentence, and justifies with parce que, plutôt que de or au lieu de. It sets the dream against real holidays in the present, uses negatives for range, and never confuses the conditional with the future or with the imperfect of a past habit.
